[334](https://gtk-rs.org#334)    /// Parses @uri_ref according to @flags and, if it is a
[335](https://gtk-rs.org#335)    /// [relative URI](#relative-and-absolute-uris), resolves it relative to @self.
[336](https://gtk-rs.org#336)    /// If the result is not a valid absolute URI, it will be discarded, and an error
[337](https://gtk-rs.org#337)    /// returned.
[338](https://gtk-rs.org#338)    /// ## `uri_ref`
[339](https://gtk-rs.org#339)    /// a string representing a relative or absolute URI
[340](https://gtk-rs.org#340)    /// ## `flags`
[341](https://gtk-rs.org#341)    /// flags describing how to parse @uri_ref
[342](https://gtk-rs.org#342)    ///
[343](https://gtk-rs.org#343)    /// # Returns
[344](https://gtk-rs.org#344)    ///
[345](https://gtk-rs.org#345)    /// a new #GUri, or NULL on error.
[346](https://gtk-rs.org#346)    #[doc(alias = "g_uri_parse_relative")]
[347](https://gtk-rs.org#347)    pub fn parse_relative(&self, uri_ref: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html), flags: [UriFlags](https://gtk-rs.org/flags.rs.html#816-877)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Uri](https://gtk-rs.org#7-183), crate::[Error](https://gtk-rs.org/error.rs.html#10-25)> {
[348](https://gtk-rs.org#348)        unsafe {
[349](https://gtk-rs.org#349)            let mut error = std::ptr::[null_mut](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ptr/fn.null_mut.html)();
[350](https://gtk-rs.org#350)            let ret = ffi::g_uri_parse_relative(
[351](https://gtk-rs.org#351)                [self](https://gtk-rs.org#347).[to_glib_none](https://gtk-rs.org/translate.rs.html#437)().0,
[352](https://gtk-rs.org#352)                [uri_ref](https://gtk-rs.org#347).[to_glib_none](https://gtk-rs.org/translate.rs.html#437)().0,
[353](https://gtk-rs.org#353)                [flags](https://gtk-rs.org#347).[into_glib](https://gtk-rs.org/translate.rs.html#334)(),
[354](https://gtk-rs.org#354)                &mut [error](https://gtk-rs.org#349),
[355](https://gtk-rs.org#355)            );
[356](https://gtk-rs.org#356)            if [error](https://gtk-rs.org#349).[is_null](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.pointer.html#method.is_null)() {
[357](https://gtk-rs.org#357)                [Ok](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok)([from_glib_full](https://gtk-rs.org/translate.rs.html#1636-1638)([ret](https://gtk-rs.org#350)))
[358](https://gtk-rs.org#358)            } else {
[359](https://gtk-rs.org#359)                [Err](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Err)([from_glib_full](https://gtk-rs.org/translate.rs.html#1636-1638)([error](https://gtk-rs.org#349)))
[360](https://gtk-rs.org#360)            }
[361](https://gtk-rs.org#361)        }
[362](https://gtk-rs.org#362)    }

[367](https://gtk-rs.org#367)    /// string that @self was parsed from. However, if the source URI was
[368](https://gtk-rs.org#368)    /// syntactically correct (according to RFC 3986), and it was parsed
[369](https://gtk-rs.org#369)    /// with [`UriFlags::ENCODED`][crate::UriFlags::ENCODED], then g_uri_to_string() is guaranteed to return
[370](https://gtk-rs.org#370)    /// a string which is at least semantically equivalent to the source

[374](https://gtk-rs.org#374)    /// or private data in its query string, and the returned string is going to be
[375](https://gtk-rs.org#375)    /// logged, then consider using g_uri_to_string_partial() to redact parts.
[376](https://gtk-rs.org#376)    ///

[534](https://gtk-rs.org#534)    ///

[871](https://gtk-rs.org#871)    /// Parses @uri_ref (which can be an
[872](https://gtk-rs.org#872)    /// [absolute or relative URI](#relative-and-absolute-uris)) according to @flags, and
[873](https://gtk-rs.org#873)    /// returns the pieces. Any component that doesn't appear in @uri_ref will be
[874](https://gtk-rs.org#874)    /// returned as [`None`] (but note that all URIs always have a path component,
[875](https://gtk-rs.org#875)    /// though it may be the empty string).
[876](https://gtk-rs.org#876)    ///
[877](https://gtk-rs.org#877)    /// If @flags contains [`UriFlags::ENCODED`][crate::UriFlags::ENCODED], then `%`-encoded characters in
[878](https://gtk-rs.org#878)    /// @uri_ref will remain encoded in the output strings. (If not,
[879](https://gtk-rs.org#879)    /// then all such characters will be decoded.) Note that decoding will
[880](https://gtk-rs.org#880)    /// only work if the URI components are ASCII or UTF-8, so you will
[881](https://gtk-rs.org#881)    /// need to use [`UriFlags::ENCODED`][crate::UriFlags::ENCODED] if they are not.
[882](https://gtk-rs.org#882)    ///
[883](https://gtk-rs.org#883)    /// Note that the [`UriFlags::HAS_PASSWORD`][crate::UriFlags::HAS_PASSWORD] and
[884](https://gtk-rs.org#884)    /// [`UriFlags::HAS_AUTH_PARAMS`][crate::UriFlags::HAS_AUTH_PARAMS] @flags are ignored by g_uri_split(),
[885](https://gtk-rs.org#885)    /// since it always returns only the full userinfo; use
[886](https://gtk-rs.org#886)    /// g_uri_split_with_user() if you want it split up.
[887](https://gtk-rs.org#887)    /// ## `uri_ref`
[888](https://gtk-rs.org#888)    /// a string containing a relative or absolute URI
[889](https://gtk-rs.org#889)    /// ## `flags`

[891](https://gtk-rs.org#891)    ///
[892](https://gtk-rs.org#892)    /// # Returns

[895](https://gtk-rs.org#895)    ///   on error.
[896](https://gtk-rs.org#896)    ///

[899](https://gtk-rs.org#899)    ///    the scheme (converted to lowercase), or [`None`]

[1154](https://gtk-rs.org#1154)    /// Unescapes a segment of an escaped string as binary data.
[1155](https://gtk-rs.org#1155)    ///
[1156](https://gtk-rs.org#1156)    /// Note that in contrast to g_uri_unescape_string(), this does allow
[1157](https://gtk-rs.org#1157)    /// nul bytes to appear in the output.
[1158](https://gtk-rs.org#1158)    ///
[1159](https://gtk-rs.org#1159)    /// If any of the characters in @illegal_characters appears as an escaped
[1160](https://gtk-rs.org#1160)    /// character in @escaped_string, then that is an error and [`None`] will be
[1161](https://gtk-rs.org#1161)    /// returned. This is useful if you want to avoid for instance having a slash
[1162](https://gtk-rs.org#1162)    /// being expanded in an escaped path element, which might confuse pathname
[1163](https://gtk-rs.org#1163)    /// handling.
[1164](https://gtk-rs.org#1164)    /// ## `escaped_string`
[1165](https://gtk-rs.org#1165)    /// A URI-escaped string
[1166](https://gtk-rs.org#1166)    /// ## `length`
[1167](https://gtk-rs.org#1167)    /// the length (in bytes) of @escaped_string to escape, or `-1` if it
[1168](https://gtk-rs.org#1168)    ///   is nul-terminated.
[1169](https://gtk-rs.org#1169)    /// ## `illegal_characters`
[1170](https://gtk-rs.org#1170)    /// a string of illegal characters
[1171](https://gtk-rs.org#1171)    ///   not to be allowed, or [`None`].
[1172](https://gtk-rs.org#1172)    ///
[1173](https://gtk-rs.org#1173)    /// # Returns

# Uri in glib - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/latest/docs/glib/struct.Uri.html

`pub struct Uri { /* private fields */ }`**crate feature**only.

`v2_66`## Expand description

The `GUri` type and related functions can be used to parse URIs into
their components, and build valid URIs from individual components.

Since `GUri` only represents absolute URIs, all `GUri`s will have a
URI scheme, so [ scheme()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Uri.html#method.scheme) will always return a non-

`NULL`
answer. Likewise, by definition, all URIs have a path component, so
[will always return a non-](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Uri.html#method.path)

`path()``NULL` string (which may
be empty).If the URI string has an
[‘authority’ component](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3986#section-3) (that
is, if the scheme is followed by `://` rather than just `:`), then the
`GUri` will contain a hostname, and possibly a port and ‘userinfo’.
Additionally, depending on how the `GUri` was constructed/parsed (for example,
using the `G_URI_FLAGS_HAS_PASSWORD` and `G_URI_FLAGS_HAS_AUTH_PARAMS` flags),
the userinfo may be split out into a username, password, and
additional authorization-related parameters.

Normally, the components of a `GUri` will have all `%`-encoded
characters decoded. However, if you construct/parse a `GUri` with
`G_URI_FLAGS_ENCODED`, then the `%`-encoding will be preserved instead in
the userinfo, path, and query fields (and in the host field if also
created with `G_URI_FLAGS_NON_DNS`). In particular, this is necessary if
the URI may contain binary data or non-UTF-8 text, or if decoding
the components might change the interpretation of the URI.

For example, with the encoded flag:

**⚠️ The following code is in c ⚠️**

```
g_autoptr(GUri) uri = g_uri_parse ("http://host/path?query=http%3A%2F%2Fhost%2Fpath%3Fparam%3Dvalue", G_URI_FLAGS_ENCODED, &err);
g_assert_cmpstr (g_uri_get_query (uri), ==, "query=http%3A%2F%2Fhost%2Fpath%3Fparam%3Dvalue");
```
While the default `%`-decoding behaviour would give:

**⚠️ The following code is in c ⚠️**

```
g_autoptr(GUri) uri = g_uri_parse ("http://host/path?query=http%3A%2F%2Fhost%2Fpath%3Fparam%3Dvalue", G_URI_FLAGS_NONE, &err);
g_assert_cmpstr (g_uri_get_query (uri), ==, "query=http://host/path?param=value");
```
During decoding, if an invalid UTF-8 string is encountered, parsing will fail with an error indicating the bad string location:

**⚠️ The following code is in c ⚠️**

```
g_autoptr(GUri) uri = g_uri_parse ("http://host/path?query=http%3A%2F%2Fhost%2Fpath%3Fbad%3D%00alue", G_URI_FLAGS_NONE, &err);
g_assert_error (err, G_URI_ERROR, G_URI_ERROR_BAD_QUERY);
```
You should pass `G_URI_FLAGS_ENCODED` or `G_URI_FLAGS_ENCODED_QUERY` if you
need to handle that case manually. In particular, if the query string
contains `=` characters that are `%`-encoded, you should let
`GLib::Uri::parse_params()` do the decoding once of the query.

`GUri` is immutable once constructed, and can safely be accessed from
multiple threads. Its reference counting is atomic.

Note that the scope of `GUri` is to help manipulate URIs in various applications,
following [RFC 3986](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3986). In particular,
it doesn’t intend to cover web browser needs, and doesn’t implement the
[WHATWG URL](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/) standard. No APIs are provided to
help prevent
[homograph attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IDN_homograph_attack), so
`GUri` is not suitable for formatting URIs for display to the user for making
security-sensitive decisions.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#relative-and-absolute-uris)Relative and absolute URIs

As defined in [RFC 3986](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3986#section-4), the
hierarchical nature of URIs means that they can either be ‘relative
references’ (sometimes referred to as ‘relative URIs’) or ‘URIs’ (for
clarity, ‘URIs’ are referred to in this documentation as
‘absolute URIs’ — although
[in contrast to RFC 3986](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3986#section-4.3),
fragment identifiers are always allowed).

Relative references have one or more components of the URI missing. In
particular, they have no scheme. Any other component, such as hostname,
query, etc. may be missing, apart from a path, which has to be specified (but
may be empty). The path may be relative, starting with `./` rather than `/`.

For example, a valid relative reference is `./path?query`,
`/?query#fragment` or `//example.com`.

Absolute URIs have a scheme specified. Any other components of the URI which
are missing are specified as explicitly unset in the URI, rather than being
resolved relative to a base URI using [ parse_relative()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Uri.html#method.parse_relative).

For example, a valid absolute URI is `file:///home/bob` or
`https://search.com?query=string`.

A `GUri` instance is always an absolute URI. A string may be an absolute URI
or a relative reference; see the documentation for individual functions as to
what forms they accept.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#parsing-uris)Parsing URIs

The most minimalist APIs for parsing URIs are [ split()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Uri.html#method.split) and

[. These split a URI into its component parts, and return the parts; the difference between the two is that](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Uri.html#method.split_with_user)

`split_with_user()`[treats the ‘userinfo’ component of the URI as a single element, while](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Uri.html#method.split)

`split()`[can (depending on the](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Uri.html#method.split_with_user)

`split_with_user()`[you pass) treat it as containing a username, password, and authentication parameters. Alternatively,](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.UriFlags.html)

`UriFlags`[can be used when you are only interested in the components that are needed to initiate a network connection to the service (scheme, host, and port).](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Uri.html#method.split_network)

`split_network()`[ parse()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Uri.html#method.parse) is similar to

[, but instead of returning individual strings, it returns a](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Uri.html#method.split)

`split()``GUri` structure (and it requires
that the URI be an absolute URI).[ resolve_relative()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Uri.html#method.resolve_relative) and

[allow you to resolve a relative URI relative to a base URI.](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Uri.html#method.parse_relative)

`parse_relative()`[takes two strings and returns a string, and](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Uri.html#method.resolve_relative)

`resolve_relative()`[takes a](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Uri.html#method.parse_relative)

`parse_relative()``GUri` and a string and returns a
`GUri`.All of the parsing functions take a [ UriFlags](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.UriFlags.html) argument describing
exactly how to parse the URI; see the documentation for that type
for more details on the specific flags that you can pass. If you
need to choose different flags based on the type of URI, you can
use

[on the URI string to check the scheme first, and use that to decide what flags to parse it with.](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Uri.html#method.peek_scheme)

`peek_scheme()`For example, you might want to use `G_URI_PARAMS_WWW_FORM` when parsing the
params for a web URI, so compare the result of [ peek_scheme()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Uri.html#method.peek_scheme)
against

`http` and `https`.[§](https://gtk-rs.org#building-uris)Building URIs

[ join()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Uri.html#method.join) and

[can be used to construct valid URI strings from a set of component strings. They are the inverse of](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Uri.html#method.join_with_user)

`join_with_user()`[and](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Uri.html#method.split)

`split()`[.](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Uri.html#method.split_with_user)

`split_with_user()`Similarly, [ build()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Uri.html#method.build) and

[can be used to construct a](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Uri.html#method.build_with_user)

`build_with_user()``GUri` from a set of component strings.As with the parsing functions, the building functions take a
[ UriFlags](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.UriFlags.html) argument. In particular, it is important to keep in mind
whether the URI components you are using are already

`%`-encoded. If so,
you must pass the `G_URI_FLAGS_ENCODED` flag.[§](https://gtk-rs.org#file-uris)`file://` URIs

Note that Windows and Unix both define special rules for parsing
`file://` URIs (involving non-UTF-8 character sets on Unix, and the
interpretation of path separators on Windows). `GUri` does not
implement these rules. Use [ filename_from_uri()](https://gtk-rs.org/fn.filename_from_uri.html) and

[if you want to properly convert between](https://gtk-rs.org/fn.filename_to_uri.html)

`filename_to_uri()``file://` URIs and local filenames.[§](https://gtk-rs.org#uri-equality)URI Equality

Note that there is no `g_uri_equal ()` function, because comparing
URIs usefully requires scheme-specific knowledge that `GUri` does
not have. `GUri` can help with normalization if you use the various
encoded [ UriFlags](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.UriFlags.html) as well as

`G_URI_FLAGS_SCHEME_NORMALIZE`
however it is not comprehensive.
For example, `data:,foo` and `data:;base64,Zm9v` resolve to the same
thing according to the `data:` URI specification which GLib does not
handle.GLib type: Shared boxed type with reference counted clone semantics.

flags describing how to parse @uri_ref

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#returns-11)Returns

a new #GUri, or NULL on error.

Returns a string representing @self.

This is not guaranteed to return a string which is identical to the
string that @self was parsed from. However, if the source URI was
syntactically correct (according to RFC 3986), and it was parsed
with [ UriFlags::ENCODED](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.UriFlags.html#associatedconstant.ENCODED), then g_uri_to_string() is guaranteed to return
a string which is at least semantically equivalent to the source
URI (according to RFC 3986).

If @self might contain sensitive details, such as authentication parameters, or private data in its query string, and the returned string is going to be logged, then consider using g_uri_to_string_partial() to redact parts.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#returns-12)Returns

a string representing @self, which the caller must free.

Escapes arbitrary data for use in a URI.

Normally all characters that are not ‘unreserved’ (i.e. ASCII alphanumerical characters plus dash, dot, underscore and tilde) are escaped. But if you specify characters in @reserved_chars_allowed they are not escaped. This is useful for the ‘reserved’ characters in the URI specification, since those are allowed unescaped in some portions of a URI.

Though technically incorrect, this will also allow escaping nul
bytes as `%``00`.

needed.  As a special case if

[is given for @escaped_string, this function will return](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None)

`None`[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None)

`None`[Source](https://gtk-rs.org/src/glib/auto/uri.rs.html#1258-1268)

[Source](https://gtk-rs.org/src/glib/auto/uri.rs.html#1258-1268)

Unescapes a whole escaped string.

If any of the characters in @illegal_characters or the NUL
character appears as an escaped character in @escaped_string, then
that is an error and [ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None) will be returned. This is useful if you
want to avoid for instance having a slash being expanded in an
escaped path element, which might confuse pathname handling.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#escaped_string-2)`escaped_string`

an escaped string to be unescaped.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#illegal_characters-2)`illegal_characters`

a string of illegal characters
not to be allowed, or [ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None).

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#returns-31)Returns

an unescaped version of @escaped_string. The returned string should be freed when no longer needed.

[33](https://gtk-rs.org#33)    /// Since `Variant`s are immutable, this does not couple the `VariantDict` with

[159](https://gtk-rs.org#159)    /// Convert this dictionary to a [`Variant`](variant/struct.Variant.html)
[160](https://gtk-rs.org#160)    ///
[161](https://gtk-rs.org#161)    /// This method converts `self` into an instance of [`Variant`](variant/struct.Variant.html)
[162](https://gtk-rs.org#162)    /// but in doing so renders it very unsafe to use.
[163](https://gtk-rs.org#163)    ///
[164](https://gtk-rs.org#164)    /// # Safety
[165](https://gtk-rs.org#165)    ///
[166](https://gtk-rs.org#166)    /// After calling this, the underlying `GVariantDict` is in a state where
[167](https://gtk-rs.org#167)    /// the only valid operations to perform as reference ones.  As such
[168](https://gtk-rs.org#168)    /// any attempt to read/update the dictionary *will* fail and emit warnings
[169](https://gtk-rs.org#169)    /// of such.
[170](https://gtk-rs.org#170)    ///
[171](https://gtk-rs.org#171)    /// You should only use this function if the extra cost of the safe function
[172](https://gtk-rs.org#172)    /// is too much for your performance critical codepaths
[173](https://gtk-rs.org#173)    pub unsafe fn end_unsafe(&self) -> [Variant](https://gtk-rs.org/variant.rs.html#119-378) {
[174](https://gtk-rs.org#174)        unsafe { [from_glib_none](https://gtk-rs.org/translate.rs.html#1627-1629)(ffi::g_variant_dict_end([self](https://gtk-rs.org#173).[to_glib_none](https://gtk-rs.org/translate.rs.html#437)().0)) }
[175](https://gtk-rs.org#175)    }
[176](https://gtk-rs.org#176)
[177](https://gtk-rs.org#177)    // rustdoc-stripper-ignore-next
[178](https://gtk-rs.org#178)    /// Convert this dictionary to a [`Variant`](variant/struct.Variant.html)
[179](https://gtk-rs.org#179)    ///
[180](https://gtk-rs.org#180)    /// This method converts `self` into an instance of [`Variant`](variant/struct.Variant.html)
[181](https://gtk-rs.org#181)    /// and then reinitialises itself in order to be safe for further use.
[182](https://gtk-rs.org#182)    ///
[183](https://gtk-rs.org#183)    /// If you are certain that nothing other than disposing of references will
[184](https://gtk-rs.org#184)    /// be done after ending the instance, you can call the
[185](https://gtk-rs.org#185)    /// [`end_unsafe()`](#method.end_unsafe) method instead to avoid the unnecessary
[186](https://gtk-rs.org#186)    /// reinitialisation of the dictionary.
[187](https://gtk-rs.org#187)    pub fn end(&self) -> [Variant](https://gtk-rs.org/variant.rs.html#119-378) {
[188](https://gtk-rs.org#188)        unsafe {
[189](https://gtk-rs.org#189)            let ret = [self](https://gtk-rs.org#187).[end_unsafe](https://gtk-rs.org#173-175)();
[190](https://gtk-rs.org#190)            // Reinitialise the dict so that we can continue safely
[191](https://gtk-rs.org#191)            ffi::g_variant_dict_init([self](https://gtk-rs.org#187).[to_glib_none](https://gtk-rs.org/translate.rs.html#437)().0, [None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None)::<[Variant](https://gtk-rs.org/variant.rs.html#119-378)>.[to_glib_none](https://gtk-rs.org/translate.rs.html#437)().0);
[192](https://gtk-rs.org#192)            [ret](https://gtk-rs.org#189)
[193](https://gtk-rs.org#193)        }
[194](https://gtk-rs.org#194)    }

[253](https://gtk-rs.org#253)    #[test]
[254](https://gtk-rs.org#254)    fn create_roundtrip() {
[255](https://gtk-rs.org#255)        let dict = VariantDict::default();
[256](https://gtk-rs.org#256)        let var: Variant = dict.to_variant();
[257](https://gtk-rs.org#257)        let _dict2: VariantDict = var.into();
[258](https://gtk-rs.org#258)    }
[259](https://gtk-rs.org#259)
[260](https://gtk-rs.org#260)    #[test]
[261](https://gtk-rs.org#261)    fn into_variant_roundtrip() {
[262](https://gtk-rs.org#262)        let dict1 = VariantDict::default();
[263](https://gtk-rs.org#263)        let dict2 = dict1.clone();
[264](https://gtk-rs.org#264)        dict1.insert_value("one", &(1u8.to_variant()));
[265](https://gtk-rs.org#265)
[266](https://gtk-rs.org#266)        assert_eq!(dict1.lookup::<u8>("one").unwrap(), Some(1u8));
[267](https://gtk-rs.org#267)        assert_eq!(dict2.lookup::<u8>("one").unwrap(), Some(1u8));
[268](https://gtk-rs.org#268)
[269](https://gtk-rs.org#269)        // Convert it into `Variant`
[270](https://gtk-rs.org#270)        let dict: Variant = dict1.into();
[271](https://gtk-rs.org#271)
[272](https://gtk-rs.org#272)        // While we can still access the `VariantDict` via `dict2`,
[273](https://gtk-rs.org#273)        // it should be empty now
[274](https://gtk-rs.org#274)        assert_eq!(dict2.lookup::<u8>("one").unwrap(), None);
[275](https://gtk-rs.org#275)
[276](https://gtk-rs.org#276)        // Convert it back

# VariantDict in glib - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/latest/docs/glib/struct.VariantDict.html

`pub struct VariantDict { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

`VariantDict` is a mutable key/value store where the keys are always
strings and the values are [ Variants](https://gtk-rs.org/variant/struct.Variant.html).

Variant dictionaries can easily be converted to/from `Variant`s of the
appropriate type.  In `glib` terms, this is a variant of the form `"a{sv}"`.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#panics)Panics

Note, pretty much all methods on this struct will panic if the
[ end_unsafe()](https://gtk-rs.org#method.end_unsafe) method was called on the instance.

GLib type: Shared boxed type with reference counted clone semantics.

### impl [VariantDict](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.VariantDict.html)

Create a new `VariantDict` optionally populating it with the given `Variant`

Since `Variant`s are immutable, this does not couple the `VariantDict` with
the input `Variant`, instead the contents are copied into the `VariantDict`.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#panics-1)Panics

This function will panic if the given `Variant` is not of the correct type.

Check if this `VariantDict` contains the given key.

Look up whether or not the given key is present, returning `true` if it
is present in `self`.

Look up a typed value from this `VariantDict`.

The given `key` is looked up in `self`.

This will return `None` if the `key` is not present in the dictionary,
and an error if the key is present but with the wrong type.

[Source](https://gtk-rs.org/src/glib/variant_dict.rs.html#87-95)

[Source](https://gtk-rs.org/src/glib/variant_dict.rs.html#87-95)

Look up and return a value from this `VariantDict`.

The given `key` is looked up in `self`.  If `expected_type` is not
`None` then it will be matched against the type of any found value.

This will return `None` if the `key` is not present in the dictionary
or if it is present but the type of the value does not match a given
`expected_type`.  Otherwise, `Some(value)` will be returned where
the `value` is an instance of [ Variant](https://gtk-rs.org/variant/struct.Variant.html).

Insert a value into the dictionary

The given `key`/`value` pair is inserted into `self`.  If a value
was previously associated with `key` then it is overwritten.

This is a convenience method which automatically calls
[ to_variant()](https://gtk-rs.org/variant/trait.ToVariant.html#method.to_variant) for you
on the given value.

If, on the other hand, you have a [ Variant](https://gtk-rs.org/variant/struct.Variant.html)
instance already, you should use the

[method instead.](https://gtk-rs.org#method.insert_value)

`insert_value()`Remove the given `key` from the dictionary.

This removes the given `key` from the dictionary, releasing the reference
on the associated value if one is present.

If a `key`/`value` pair was removed from the dictionary, `true` is
returned.  If `key` was not present then `false` is returned instead.

[Source](https://gtk-rs.org/src/glib/variant_dict.rs.html#173-175)#### pub unsafe fn [end_unsafe](https://gtk-rs.org#method.end_unsafe)(&self) -> [Variant](https://gtk-rs.org/variant/struct.Variant.html)

[Source](https://gtk-rs.org/src/glib/variant_dict.rs.html#173-175)

#### pub unsafe fn [end_unsafe](https://gtk-rs.org#method.end_unsafe)(&self) -> [Variant](https://gtk-rs.org/variant/struct.Variant.html)

Convert this dictionary to a `Variant`

This method converts `self` into an instance of [ Variant](https://gtk-rs.org/variant/struct.Variant.html)
but in doing so renders it very unsafe to use.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#safety)Safety

After calling this, the underlying `GVariantDict` is in a state where
the only valid operations to perform as reference ones.  As such
any attempt to read/update the dictionary *will* fail and emit warnings
of such.

You should only use this function if the extra cost of the safe function is too much for your performance critical codepaths

Convert this dictionary to a `Variant`

This method converts `self` into an instance of [ Variant](https://gtk-rs.org/variant/struct.Variant.html)
and then reinitialises itself in order to be safe for further use.

If you are certain that nothing other than disposing of references will
be done after ending the instance, you can call the
[ end_unsafe()](https://gtk-rs.org#method.end_unsafe) method instead to avoid the unnecessary
reinitialisation of the dictionary.

# glib::subclass - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/latest/docs/glib/subclass/index.html

## Expand description

Module containing infrastructure for subclassing `GObject`s and registering boxed types.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#example-for-registering-a-glibobject-subclass)Example for registering a `glib::Object` subclass

The following code implements a subclass of `glib::Object` with a
string-typed “name” property.

```
use glib::prelude::*;
use glib::subclass;
use glib::subclass::prelude::*;
use glib::{Variant, VariantType};
use std::cell::{Cell, RefCell};
#[derive(Debug, Eq, PartialEq, Clone, Copy, glib::Enum)]
#[repr(u32)]
// type_name: GType name of the enum (mandatory)
#[enum_type(name = "SimpleObjectAnimal")]
enum Animal {
    Goat = 0,
    #[enum_value(name = "The Dog")]
    Dog = 1,
    // name: the name of the GEnumValue (optional), default to the enum name in CamelCase
    // nick: the nick of the GEnumValue (optional), default to the enum name in kebab-case
    #[enum_value(name = "The Cat", nick = "chat")]
    Cat = 2,
}
impl Default for Animal {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Animal::Goat
    }
}
#[glib::flags(name = "MyFlags")]
enum MyFlags {
    #[flags_value(name = "Flag A", nick = "nick-a")]
    A = 0b00000001,
    #[flags_value(name = "Flag B")]
    B = 0b00000010,
    #[flags_value(skip)]
    AB = Self::A.bits() | Self::B.bits(),
    C = 0b00000100,
}
impl Default for MyFlags {
    fn default() -> Self {
        MyFlags::A
    }
}
// Implementing a GObject subclass requires two Rust types
// working closely in tandem.
mod imp {
    use super::*;
    // This is the struct containing all state carried with
    // the new type. It will be stored in the GType's instance-private data.
    // Generally this has to make use of interior mutability.
    // If it implements the `Default` trait, then `Self::default()`
    // will be called every time a new instance is created.
    #[derive(Default)]
    pub struct SimpleObject {
        name: RefCell<Option<String>>,
        animal: Cell<Animal>,
        flags: Cell<MyFlags>,
        variant: RefCell<Option<Variant>>,
    }
    // ObjectSubclass is the trait that defines the new type and
    // contains all information needed by the GObject type system,
    // including the new type's name, parent type, etc. The implementation
    // struct is mapped to the type's instance-private data. This information is
    // registered with the Glib runtime in the `register_type()` function.
    // If you do not want to implement `Default`, you can provide
    // a `new()` method.
    #[glib::object_subclass]
    impl ObjectSubclass for SimpleObject {
        // This type name must be unique per process.
        const NAME: &'static str = "SimpleObject";
        // The wrapper around the raw GType instance struct
        // (of type `ObjectSubclass::Instance`) providing memory management functionality
        // and defining class relationships in terms of Rust types
        type Type = super::SimpleObject;
        // The parent type this one is inheriting from.
        // Optional, if not specified it defaults to `glib::Object`
        type ParentType = glib::Object;
        // Interfaces this type implements.
        // Optional, if not specified it defaults to `()`
        type Interfaces = ();
    }
    // Trait used to override virtual methods of glib::Object. It requires
    // that the associated `Type` implements the `IsA<Object>` trait declaring that
    // it can be upcasted to glib::Object, ensuring that virtual methods defined by
    // a class can only be overridden by its subclasses.
    //
    // The Rust bindings for GObject generate function wrappers proxying these
    // methods of the private instance struct and initialize the subclass's vtable
    // with those wrappers during object instantiation.
    impl ObjectImpl for SimpleObject {
        // Called once in the very beginning to list all properties of this class.
        fn properties() -> &'static [glib::ParamSpec] {
            use std::sync::OnceLock;
            static PROPERTIES: OnceLock<Vec<glib::ParamSpec>> = OnceLock::new();
            PROPERTIES.get_or_init(|| {
                vec![
                    glib::ParamSpecString::builder("name")
                        .build(),
                    glib::ParamSpecEnum::builder::<Animal>("animal")
                        .build(),
                    glib::ParamSpecFlags::builder::<MyFlags>("flags")
                        .build(),
                    glib::ParamSpecVariant::builder("variant", glib::VariantTy::ANY)
                        .build(),
                ]
            })
        }
        // Called whenever a property is set on this instance. The id
        // is the same as the index of the property in the PROPERTIES array.
        fn set_property(&self, _id: usize, value: &glib::Value, pspec: &glib::ParamSpec) {
            match pspec.name() {
                "name" => {
                    let name = value
                        .get()
                        .expect("type conformity checked by `Object::set_property`");
                    self.name.replace(name);
                },
                "animal" => {
                    let animal = value
                        .get()
                        .expect("type conformity checked by `Object::set_property`");
                    self.animal.replace(animal);
                },
                "flags" => {
                    let flags = value
                        .get()
                        .expect("type conformity checked by `Object::set_property`");
                    self.flags.replace(flags);
                },
                "variant" => {
                    let variant = value
                        .get()
                        .expect("type conformity checked by `Object::set_property`");
                    self.variant.replace(variant);
                },
                _ => unimplemented!(),
            }
        }
        // Called whenever a property is retrieved from this instance. The id
        // is the same as the index of the property in the PROPERTIES array.
        fn property(&self, _id: usize, pspec: &glib::ParamSpec) -> glib::Value {
            match pspec.name() {
                "name" => self.name.borrow().to_value(),
                "animal" => self.animal.get().to_value(),
                "flags" => self.flags.get().to_value(),
                "variant" => self.variant.borrow().to_value(),
                _ => unimplemented!(),
            }
        }
        // Called right after construction of the instance.
        fn constructed(&self) {
            // Chain up to the parent type's implementation of this virtual
            // method.
            self.parent_constructed();
            // And here we could do our own initialization.
        }
    }
}
// Create a type implementing:
// - the basic traits to support Rust memory management functionality on the
//   raw GType instance pointer defined above
// - the core `IsA<Object>` trait declaring that `SimpleObject` is a subclass of `Object`
// - any public methods on the subclass
// This type provides the external interface to the `SimpleObject` class. It is
// analogous to an opaque C pointer `SimpleObject*` that would be declared
// in the public header file simpleobject.h if one were to define `SimpleObject`
// in simpleobject.c. The methods defined here correspond to the functions
// declared in simpleobject.h.
//
glib::wrapper! {
    pub struct SimpleObject(ObjectSubclass<imp::SimpleObject>);
}
impl SimpleObject {
    // Create an object instance of the new type.
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        glib::Object::new()
    }
}
// This is the Rust analog of a C declaration like
//
// /* simpleobject.h */
// #include <glib-object.h>
// G_DECLARE_FINAL_TYPE (SimpleObject, simple_object, ...)
// SimpleObject* simple_object_new();
//
// The Rust structs defined above produce roughly the following instance memory layout:
//
//       vtable populated with functions proxying imp::SimpleObject::ObjectImpl
//       during class_init (see `unsafe impl<T: ObjectImpl>IsSubclassable<T> for Object`)
//                                      |
//                                     ffi::GObjectClass
//                                      ^
//                                      |
//                                     ffi::GObject (first member of instance struct)
//                                      |
// |--private data (imp::SimpleObject)--|--instance struct (basic::InstanceStruct)--|
//                                      ^
//                                      |
//                                      |
//                                 SimpleObject
pub fn main() {
    let obj = SimpleObject::new();
    // Get the name property and change its value.
    // The `ObjectExt` trait provides implementations of
    // `glib::Object`'s public methods on the (wrappers of)
    // GObject subclasses. These invoke the corresponding GObject
    // virtual methods across the FFI interface, which in turn proxy
    // the `ObjectImpl` methods on the private instance struct above.
    assert_eq!(obj.property::<Option<String>>("name"), None);
    obj.set_property("name", "test");
    assert_eq!(&obj.property::<String>("name"), "test");
    assert_eq!(obj.property::<Animal>("animal"), Animal::Goat);
    obj.set_property("animal", Animal::Cat);
    assert_eq!(obj.property::<Animal>("animal"), Animal::Cat);
    assert_eq!(obj.property::<MyFlags>("flags"), MyFlags::A);
    obj.set_property("flags", MyFlags::B);
    assert_eq!(obj.property::<MyFlags>("flags"), MyFlags::B);
}
```
[§](https://gtk-rs.org#example-for-registering-a-glibobject-subclass-within-a-module)Example for registering a `glib::Object` subclass within a module

The following code implements a subclass of `glib::Object` and registers it as
a dynamic type.

```
use glib::prelude::*;
use glib::subclass::prelude::*;
pub mod imp {
    use super::*;
    // SimpleModuleObject is a dynamic type.
    #[derive(Default)]
    pub struct SimpleModuleObject;
    #[glib::object_subclass]
    #[object_subclass_dynamic]
    impl ObjectSubclass for SimpleModuleObject {
        const NAME: &'static str = "SimpleModuleObject";
        type Type = super::SimpleModuleObject;
    }
    impl ObjectImpl for SimpleModuleObject {}
    // SimpleTypeModule is the type module within the object subclass is registered as a dynamic type.
    #[derive(Default)]
    pub struct SimpleTypeModule;
    #[glib::object_subclass]
    impl ObjectSubclass for SimpleTypeModule {
        const NAME: &'static str = "SimpleTypeModule";
        type Type = super::SimpleTypeModule;
        type ParentType = glib::TypeModule;
        type Interfaces = (glib::TypePlugin,);
    }
    impl ObjectImpl for SimpleTypeModule {}
    impl TypeModuleImpl for SimpleTypeModule {
        /// Loads the module and registers the object subclass as a dynamic type.
        fn load(&self) -> bool {
            SimpleModuleObject::on_implementation_load(self.obj().upcast_ref::<glib::TypeModule>())
        }
        /// Unloads the module.
        fn unload(&self) {
            SimpleModuleObject::on_implementation_unload(self.obj().upcast_ref::<glib::TypeModule>());
        }
    }
    impl TypePluginImpl for SimpleTypeModule {}
}
// Optionally, defines a wrapper type to make SimpleModuleObject more ergonomic to use from Rust.
glib::wrapper! {
    pub struct SimpleModuleObject(ObjectSubclass<imp::SimpleModuleObject>);
}
// Optionally, defines a wrapper type to make SimpleTypeModule more ergonomic to use from Rust.
glib::wrapper! {
    pub struct SimpleTypeModule(ObjectSubclass<imp::SimpleTypeModule>)
    @extends glib::TypeModule, @implements glib::TypePlugin;
}
impl SimpleTypeModule {
    // Creates an object instance of the new type.
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        glib::Object::new()
    }
}
pub fn main() {
    let simple_type_module = SimpleTypeModule::new();
    // at this step, SimpleTypeModule has not been loaded therefore
    // SimpleModuleObject must not be registered yet.
    let simple_module_object_type = imp::SimpleModuleObject::type_();
    assert!(!simple_module_object_type.is_valid());
    // simulates the GLib type system to load the module.
    TypeModuleExt::use_(&simple_type_module);
    // at this step, SimpleModuleObject must have been registered.
    let simple_module_object_type = imp::SimpleModuleObject::type_();
    assert!(simple_module_object_type.is_valid());
}
```
[§](https://gtk-rs.org#example-for-registering-a-glibobject-subclass-within-a-plugin)Example for registering a `glib::Object` subclass within a plugin

The following code implements a subclass of `glib::Object` and registers it as
a dynamic type.

```
use glib::prelude::*;
use glib::subclass::prelude::*;
pub mod imp {
    use super::*;
    // SimplePluginObject is a dynamic type.
    #[derive(Default)]
    pub struct SimplePluginObject;
    #[glib::object_subclass]
    #[object_subclass_dynamic(plugin_type = super::SimpleTypePlugin)]
    impl ObjectSubclass for SimplePluginObject {
        const NAME: &'static str = "SimplePluginObject";
        type Type = super::SimplePluginObject;
    }
    impl ObjectImpl for SimplePluginObject {}
    // SimpleTypePlugin is the type plugin within the object subclass is registered as a dynamic type.
    #[derive(Default)]
    pub struct SimpleTypePlugin {
        type_info: std::cell::Cell<Option<glib::TypeInfo>>
    }
    #[glib::object_subclass]
    impl ObjectSubclass for SimpleTypePlugin {
        const NAME: &'static str = "SimpleTypePlugin";
        type Type = super::SimpleTypePlugin;
        type Interfaces = (glib::TypePlugin,);
    }
    impl ObjectImpl for SimpleTypePlugin {}
    impl TypePluginImpl for SimpleTypePlugin {
        /// Uses the plugin and registers the object subclass as a dynamic type.
        fn use_plugin(&self) {
            SimplePluginObject::on_implementation_load(self.obj().as_ref());
        }
        /// Unuses the plugin.
        fn unuse_plugin(&self) {
            SimplePluginObject::on_implementation_unload(self.obj().as_ref());
        }
        /// Returns type information about the object subclass registered as a dynamic type.
        fn complete_type_info(&self, _type_: glib::Type) -> (glib::TypeInfo, glib::TypeValueTable) {
            assert!(self.type_info.get().is_some());
            // returns type info.
            (self.type_info.get().unwrap(), glib::TypeValueTable::default())
        }
    }
    impl TypePluginRegisterImpl for SimpleTypePlugin {
        fn register_dynamic_type(&self, parent_type: glib::Type, type_name: &str, type_info: &glib::TypeInfo, flags: glib::TypeFlags) -> glib::Type {
            let type_ = glib::Type::from_name(type_name).unwrap_or_else(|| {
                glib::Type::register_dynamic(parent_type, type_name, self.obj().upcast_ref::<glib::TypePlugin>(), flags)
            });
            if type_.is_valid() {
                // saves type info.
                self.type_info.set(Some(*type_info));
            }
            type_
        }
    }
}
// Optionally, defines a wrapper type to make SimplePluginObject more ergonomic to use from Rust.
glib::wrapper! {
    pub struct SimplePluginObject(ObjectSubclass<imp::SimplePluginObject>);
}
// Optionally, defines a wrapper type to make SimpleTypePlugin more ergonomic to use from Rust.
glib::wrapper! {
    pub struct SimpleTypePlugin(ObjectSubclass<imp::SimpleTypePlugin>)
    @implements glib::TypePlugin;
}
impl SimpleTypePlugin {
    // Creates an object instance of the new type.
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        glib::Object::new()
    }
}
pub fn main() {
    let simple_type_plugin = SimpleTypePlugin::new();
    // at this step, SimpleTypePlugin has not been used therefore
    // SimplePluginObject must not be registered yet.
    let simple_plugin_object_type = imp::SimplePluginObject::type_();
    assert!(!simple_plugin_object_type.is_valid());
    // simulates the GLib type system to use the plugin.
    TypePluginExt::use_(&simple_type_plugin);
    // at this step, SimplePluginObject must have been registered.
    let simple_plugin_object_type = imp::SimplePluginObject::type_();
    assert!(simple_plugin_object_type.is_valid());
}
```
//! # Example for registering a boxed type for a Rust struct

The following code boxed type for a tuple struct around `String` and uses it in combination
with `glib::Value`.

```
use glib::prelude::*;
use glib::subclass;
use glib::subclass::prelude::*;
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, glib::Boxed)]
#[boxed_type(name = "MyBoxed")]
struct MyBoxed(String);
pub fn main() {
    assert!(MyBoxed::static_type().is_valid());
    let b = MyBoxed(String::from("abc"));
    let v = b.to_value();
    let b2 = v.get::<&MyBoxed>().unwrap();
    assert_eq!(&b, b2);
}
```

## Modules[§](https://gtk-rs.org#modules)

- [basic](https://gtk-rs.org/basic/index.html)
- This module contains basic instance and class structs to be used for
`GObject`subclasses that don’t require any additional data in these structs and don’t provide any new virtual methods.
- [boxed](https://gtk-rs.org/boxed/index.html)
- Module for registering boxed types for Rust types.
- [interface](https://gtk-rs.org/interface/index.html)
- [object](https://gtk-rs.org/object/index.html)
- Module that contains all types needed for creating a direct subclass of `GObject`or implementing virtual methods of it.
- [prelude](https://gtk-rs.org/prelude/index.html)
- Prelude that re-exports all important traits from this crate.
- [shared](https://gtk-rs.org/shared/index.html)
- Module for registering shared types for Rust types.
- [signal](https://gtk-rs.org/signal/index.html)
- [type_](https://gtk-rs.org/type_module/index.html)- module
- [type_](https://gtk-rs.org/type_plugin/index.html)- plugin
- [types](https://gtk-rs.org/types/index.html)
- Module that contains the basic infrastructure for subclassing `GObject`.

[264](https://gtk-rs.org#264)/// Registers a `glib::Type` ID for `T::Class` as a dynamic type.
[265](https://gtk-rs.org#265)///
[266](https://gtk-rs.org#266)/// An object interface must be explicitly registered as a dynamic type when
[267](https://gtk-rs.org#267)/// the system loads the implementation by calling [`TypePluginImpl::use_`] or
[268](https://gtk-rs.org#268)/// more specifically [`TypeModuleImpl::load`]. Therefore, unlike for object
[269](https://gtk-rs.org#269)/// interfaces registered as static types, object interfaces registered as
[270](https://gtk-rs.org#270)/// dynamic types can be registered several times.

# Trait ObjectInterfaceType

[Source](../../../src/glib/subclass/interface.rs.html#64-70) ```
pub unsafe trait ObjectInterfaceType {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[type_](#tymethod.type_)() -> [Type](../../types/struct.Type.html);
}

## Expand description

Returns the `glib::Type` ID of the interface.

This will register the type with the type system on the first call.

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# ParamSpec in glib - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/latest/docs/glib/struct.ParamSpec.html

`pub struct ParamSpec { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

`GParamSpec` encapsulates the metadata required to specify parameters, such as `GObject` properties.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#parameter-names)Parameter names

A property name consists of one or more segments consisting of ASCII letters
and digits, separated by either the `-` or `_` character. The first
character of a property name must be a letter. These are the same rules as
for signal naming (see `signal_new()`).

When creating and looking up a `GParamSpec`, either separator can be
used, but they cannot be mixed. Using `-` is considerably more
efficient, and is the ‘canonical form’. Using `_` is discouraged.

This is an Abstract Base Class, you cannot instantiate it.

GLib type: Shared boxed type with reference counted clone semantics.

# register_interface in glib::subclass::interface - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/latest/docs/glib/subclass/interface/fn.register_interface.html

`pub fn register_interface<T: `[ObjectInterface](https://gtk-rs.org/trait.ObjectInterface.html)>() -> [Type](https://gtk-rs.org/types/struct.Type.html)## Expand description

Register a `glib::Type` ID for `T::Class`.

This must be called only once and will panic on a second call.

The [ object_interface!](https://gtk-rs.org/macro.object_interface.html) macro will create a

`type_()` function around this, which will
ensure that it’s only ever called once.

# glib::subclass::types - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/latest/docs/glib/subclass/types/index.html

## Expand description

Module that contains the basic infrastructure for subclassing `GObject`.

## Structs[§](https://gtk-rs.org#structs)

- [Initializing](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.InitializingObject.html)- Object
- An object that is currently being initialized.
- [Initializing](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.InitializingType.html)- Type
- A newly registered `glib::Type`that is currently still being initialized.
- [Type](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.TypeData.html)- Data
- Type-specific data that is filled in during type creation.

## Traits[§](https://gtk-rs.org#traits)

- [Class](https://gtk-rs.org/trait.ClassStruct.html)- Struct
- Trait implemented by structs that implement a `GObject`C class struct.
- [From](https://gtk-rs.org/trait.FromObject.html)- Object
- Helper trait for macros to access a subclass or its wrapper.
- [Instance](https://gtk-rs.org/trait.InstanceStruct.html)- Struct
- Trait implemented by structs that implement a `GObject`C instance struct.
- [Instance](https://gtk-rs.org/trait.InstanceStructExt.html)- Struct - Ext
- Trait implemented by any type implementing `InstanceStruct`to return the implementation, private Rust struct.
- [Interface](https://gtk-rs.org/trait.InterfaceList.html)- List
- Trait for a type list of interfaces.
- [Interface](https://gtk-rs.org/trait.InterfaceStruct.html)- Struct
- Trait implemented by structs that implement a `GTypeInterface`C class struct.
- [IsImplementable](https://gtk-rs.org/trait.IsImplementable.html)
- Trait for implementable interfaces.
- [IsSubclassable](https://gtk-rs.org/trait.IsSubclassable.html)
- Trait for subclassable class structs.
- [IsSubclassable](https://gtk-rs.org/trait.IsSubclassableExt.html)- Ext
- [Object](https://gtk-rs.org/trait.ObjectSubclass.html)- Subclass
- The central trait for subclassing a `GObject`type.
- [Object](https://gtk-rs.org/trait.ObjectSubclassExt.html)- Subclass - Ext
- Extension methods for all `ObjectSubclass`impls.
- [Object](https://gtk-rs.org/trait.ObjectSubclassIsExt.html)- Subclass - IsExt
- Trait implemented by any type implementing `ObjectSubclassIs`to return the implementation, private Rust struct.
- [Object](https://gtk-rs.org/trait.ObjectSubclassType.html)- Subclass - Type
- Type methods required for an `ObjectSubclass`

## Functions[§](https://gtk-rs.org#functions)

- [register_](https://gtk-rs.org/fn.register_dynamic_type.html)- dynamic_ - type
- Registers a `glib::Type`ID for`T`as a dynamic type.
- [register_](https://gtk-rs.org/fn.register_type.html)- type
- Register a `glib::Type`ID for`T`.

[92](https://gtk-rs.org#92)/// Offset `ptr` by `offset` *bytes* and cast the result to `*const U`.
[93](https://gtk-rs.org#93)///
[94](https://gtk-rs.org#94)/// The result must be a correctly aligned pointer to a valid value of type `U`.
[95](https://gtk-rs.org#95)///
[96](https://gtk-rs.org#96)/// # Panics:
[97](https://gtk-rs.org#97)///
[98](https://gtk-rs.org#98)/// This function panics if debug assertions are enabled if adding `offset` causes `ptr` to
[99](https://gtk-rs.org#99)/// overflow or if the resulting pointer is not correctly aligned.
[100](https://gtk-rs.org#100)#[inline]
[101](https://gtk-rs.org#101)fn offset_ptr_by_bytes<T, U>(ptr: *const T, offset: [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.isize.html)) -> *const U {
[102](https://gtk-rs.org#102)    let ptr = [ptr](https://gtk-rs.org#101).[expose_provenance](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.pointer.html#method.expose_provenance)();
[103](https://gtk-rs.org#103)    let ptr = if [offset](https://gtk-rs.org#101) < 0 {
[104](https://gtk-rs.org#104)        [ptr](https://gtk-rs.org#102) - (-[offset](https://gtk-rs.org#101)) as [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)
[105](https://gtk-rs.org#105)    } else {
[106](https://gtk-rs.org#106)        [ptr](https://gtk-rs.org#102) + [offset](https://gtk-rs.org#101) as [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)
[107](https://gtk-rs.org#107)    };
[108](https://gtk-rs.org#108)    let ptr: *const U = std::ptr::[with_exposed_provenance](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ptr/fn.with_exposed_provenance.html)([ptr](https://gtk-rs.org#103));
[109](https://gtk-rs.org#109)    [debug_assert!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/macro.debug_assert.html)(ptr.is_aligned());
[110](https://gtk-rs.org#110)    [ptr](https://gtk-rs.org#108)

[387](https://gtk-rs.org#387)// Generates all the InterfaceList impls for interface_lists of arbitrary sizes based on a list of type
[388](https://gtk-rs.org#388)// parameters like A B C. It would generate the impl then for (A, B) and (A, B, C).
[389](https://gtk-rs.org#389)macro_rules! interface_list_trait(
[390](https://gtk-rs.org#390)    ($name1:ident, $name2: ident, $($name:ident),*) => (
[391](https://gtk-rs.org#391)        interface_list_trait!(__impl $name1, $name2; $($name),*);

[394](https://gtk-rs.org#394)        interface_list_trait_impl!($($name),+);
[395](https://gtk-rs.org#395)        interface_list_trait!(__impl $($name),+ , $name1; $($name2),*);
[396](https://gtk-rs.org#396)    );
[397](https://gtk-rs.org#397)    (__impl $($name:ident),+; $name1:ident) => (
[398](https://gtk-rs.org#398)        interface_list_trait_impl!($($name),+);
[399](https://gtk-rs.org#399)        interface_list_trait_impl!($($name),+, $name1);

[641](https://gtk-rs.org#641)    ///
[642](https://gtk-rs.org#642)    /// By default, trying to register a type with a name that was registered before will panic. If
[643](https://gtk-rs.org#643)    /// this is set to `true` then a new name will be selected by appending a counter.
[644](https://gtk-rs.org#644)    ///
[645](https://gtk-rs.org#645)    /// This is useful for defining new types in Rust library crates that might be linked multiple
[646](https://gtk-rs.org#646)    /// times in the same process.
[647](https://gtk-rs.org#647)    ///
[648](https://gtk-rs.org#648)    /// A consequence of setting this to `true` is that it's not guaranteed that
[649](https://gtk-rs.org#649)    /// `glib::Type::from_name(Self::NAME).unwrap() == Self::type_()`.
[650](https://gtk-rs.org#650)    ///
[651](https://gtk-rs.org#651)    /// Note that this is not allowed for dynamic types. If a dynamic type is registered and a type
[652](https://gtk-rs.org#652)    /// with that name exists already, it is assumed that they're the same.
[653](https://gtk-rs.org#653)    ///
[654](https://gtk-rs.org#654)    /// Optional.

[1003](https://gtk-rs.org#1003)        let mut data = T::[type_data](https://gtk-rs.org#581)();

[1114](https://gtk-rs.org#1114)/// Registers a `glib::Type` ID for `T` as a dynamic type.
[1115](https://gtk-rs.org#1115)///
[1116](https://gtk-rs.org#1116)/// An object subclass must be explicitly registered as a dynamic type when the

# FromGlibPtrBorrow in glib::translate - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/latest/docs/glib/translate/trait.FromGlibPtrBorrow.html

`pub trait FromGlibPtrBorrow<P: `[Ptr](https://gtk-rs.org/trait.Ptr.html)>: [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {
    // Provided method
    unsafe fn [from_glib_borrow](https://gtk-rs.org#method.from_glib_borrow)(_ptr: P) -> [Borrowed](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Borrowed.html)<Self> { ... }
}## Expand description

Translate from a pointer type by borrowing, without affecting the refcount.

The purpose of this trait is to access values inside callbacks without changing their reference status. The obtained borrow must not be accessed outside of the scope of the callback, and called procedures must not store any references to the underlying data. Safe Rust code must never obtain a mutable Rust reference.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#safety)Safety

The implementation of this trait as well as the returned type must satisfy the same constraints together. They must not take ownership of the underlying value, copy it, and should not change its reference count. If it does, it must properly release obtained references.

The returned value, when dropped, must leave the underlying value in the same state as before from_glib_borrow was called:

- it must not be dropped,
- it must be the same type of reference, e.g. still floating.

For more information, refer to module level documentation.

## Provided Methods[§](https://gtk-rs.org#provided-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://gtk-rs.org#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# InstanceStruct in glib::subclass::types - Rust

`pub unsafe trait InstanceStruct: `[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) + 'static {

    // Provided method
    fn [instance_init](https://gtk-rs.org#method.instance_init)(&mut self) { ... }
}## Expand description

Trait implemented by structs that implement a `GObject` C instance struct.

The struct must be `#[repr(C)]` and have the parent type’s instance struct
as the first field.

See [ basic::InstanceStruct](https://gtk-rs.org/basic/struct.InstanceStruct.html) for a basic implementation of this that can
be used most of the time and should only not be used if additional fields are
required in the instance struct.

Binding crates should use traits for adding methods to this struct. Only methods explicitly safe

# register_type in glib::subclass::types - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/latest/docs/glib/subclass/types/fn.register_type.html

`pub fn register_type<T: `[ObjectSubclass](https://gtk-rs.org/trait.ObjectSubclass.html)>() -> [Type](https://gtk-rs.org/types/struct.Type.html)## Expand description

Register a `glib::Type` ID for `T`.

This must be called only once and will panic on a second call.

The [ object_subclass!](https://gtk-rs.org/macro.object_subclass.html) macro will create a

`type_()` function around this, which will
ensure that it’s only ever called once.

[23](https://gtk-rs.org#23)
[24](https://gtk-rs.org#24)    // rustdoc-stripper-ignore-next
[25](https://gtk-rs.org#25)    /// Allow name conflicts for this boxed type.
[26](https://gtk-rs.org#26)    ///
[27](https://gtk-rs.org#27)    /// By default, trying to register a type with a name that was registered before will panic. If
[28](https://gtk-rs.org#28)    /// this is set to `true` then a new name will be selected by appending a counter.
[29](https://gtk-rs.org#29)    ///
[30](https://gtk-rs.org#30)    /// This is useful for defining new types in Rust library crates that might be linked multiple
[31](https://gtk-rs.org#31)    /// times in the same process.
[32](https://gtk-rs.org#32)    ///
[33](https://gtk-rs.org#33)    /// A consequence of setting this to `true` is that it's not guaranteed that
[34](https://gtk-rs.org#34)    /// `glib::Type::from_name(Self::NAME).unwrap() == Self::static_type()`.
[35](https://gtk-rs.org#35)    ///
[36](https://gtk-rs.org#36)    /// Optional.
[37](https://gtk-rs.org#37)    const ALLOW_NAME_CONFLICT: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html) = false;
[38](https://gtk-rs.org#38)}

# register_boxed_type in glib::subclass::boxed - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/latest/docs/glib/subclass/boxed/fn.register_boxed_type.html

## Expand description

Register a boxed `glib::Type` ID for `T`.

This must be called only once and will panic on a second call.

See [ Boxed!](https://gtk-rs.org/derive.Boxed.html) for defining a function that ensures that
this is only called once and returns the type id.

# BorrowedObject in glib::object - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/latest/docs/glib/object/struct.BorrowedObject.html

`pub struct BorrowedObject<'a, T> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Borrowed reference to an object of type `T`.

This dereferences into `&T`.

## Implementations[§](https://gtk-rs.org#implementations)

# ObjectImplRef in glib::subclass - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/latest/docs/glib/subclass/struct.ObjectImplRef.html

`pub struct ObjectImplRef<T: `[ObjectSubclass](https://gtk-rs.org/types/trait.ObjectSubclass.html)>(/* private fields */);## Expand description

Reference-counted wrapper around an [ ObjectSubclass](https://gtk-rs.org/types/trait.ObjectSubclass.html) reference.

This can be used for passing into closures as strong or weak reference without manually going from the implementation type to the instance type and back.

## Expand description

Error codes returned by character set conversion routines.

## This enum is marked as non-exhaustive

Conversion between the requested character sets is not supported.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.IllegalSequence)

Invalid byte sequence in conversion input; or the character sequence could not be represented in the target character set.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Failed)

### Failed

Conversion failed for some reason.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.PartialInput)

### PartialInput

Partial character sequence at end of input.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.BadUri)

### BadUri

URI is invalid.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.NotAbsolutePath)

### NotAbsolutePath

Pathname is not an absolute path.

### NoMemory

No memory available. Since: 2.40

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.EmbeddedNul)

### EmbeddedNul

An embedded NUL character is present in conversion output where a NUL-terminated string is expected. Since: 2.56

# FileError in glib - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/latest/docs/glib/enum.FileError.html

```
#[non_exhaustive]pub enum FileError {
```
## Show 25 variants

    Exist,
    Isdir,
    Acces,
    Nametoolong,
    Noent,
    Notdir,
    Nxio,
    Nodev,
    Rofs,
    Txtbsy,
    Fault,
    Loop,
    Nospc,
    Nomem,
    Mfile,
    Nfile,
    Badf,
    Inval,
    Pipe,
    Again,
    Intr,
    Io,
    Perm,
    Nosys,
    Failed,
}## Expand description

Values corresponding to @errno codes returned from file operations on UNIX. Unlike @errno codes, GFileError values are available on all systems, even Windows. The exact meaning of each code depends on what sort of file operation you were performing; the UNIX documentation gives more details. The following error code descriptions come from the GNU C Library manual, and are under the copyright of that manual.

It’s not very portable to make detailed assumptions about exactly which errors will be returned from a given operation. Some errors don’t occur on some systems, etc., sometimes there are subtle differences in when a system will report a given error, etc.

## Variants (Non-exhaustive)[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variants)

## This enum is marked as non-exhaustive

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Exist)

### Exist

Operation not permitted; only the owner of the file (or other resource) or processes with special privileges can perform the operation.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Isdir)

### Isdir

File is a directory; you cannot open a directory for writing, or create or remove hard links to it.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Acces)

### Acces

Permission denied; the file permissions do not allow the attempted operation.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Nametoolong)

### Nametoolong

Filename too long.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Noent)

### Noent

No such file or directory. This is a “file doesn’t exist” error for ordinary files that are referenced in contexts where they are expected to already exist.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Notdir)

### Notdir

A file that isn’t a directory was specified when a directory is required.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Nxio)

### Nxio

No such device or address. The system tried to use the device represented by a file you specified, and it couldn’t find the device. This can mean that the device file was installed incorrectly, or that the physical device is missing or not correctly attached to the computer.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Nodev)

### Nodev

The underlying file system of the specified file does not support memory mapping.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Rofs)

### Rofs

The directory containing the new link can’t be modified because it’s on a read-only file system.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Txtbsy)

### Txtbsy

Text file busy.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Fault)

### Fault

You passed in a pointer to bad memory. (GLib won’t reliably return this, don’t pass in pointers to bad memory.)

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Loop)

### Loop

Too many levels of symbolic links were encountered in looking up a file name. This often indicates a cycle of symbolic links.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Nospc)

### Nospc

No space left on device; write operation on a file failed because the disk is full.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Nomem)

### Nomem

No memory available. The system cannot allocate more virtual memory because its capacity is full.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Mfile)

### Mfile

The current process has too many files open and can’t open any more. Duplicate descriptors do count toward this limit.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Nfile)

### Nfile

There are too many distinct file openings in the entire system.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Badf)

### Badf

Bad file descriptor; for example, I/O on a descriptor that has been closed or reading from a descriptor open only for writing (or vice versa).

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Inval)

### Inval

Invalid argument. This is used to indicate various kinds of problems with passing the wrong argument to a library function.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Pipe)

### Pipe

Broken pipe; there is no process reading from the other end of a pipe. Every library function that returns this error code also generates a ‘SIGPIPE’ signal; this signal terminates the program if not handled or blocked. Thus, your program will never actually see this code unless it has handled or blocked ‘SIGPIPE’.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Again)

### Again

Resource temporarily unavailable; the call might work if you try again later.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Intr)

### Intr

Interrupted function call; an asynchronous signal occurred and prevented completion of the call. When this happens, you should try the call again.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Io)

### Io

Input/output error; usually used for physical read or write errors. i.e. the disk or other physical device hardware is returning errors.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Perm)

### Perm

Operation not permitted; only the owner of the file (or other resource) or processes with special privileges can perform the operation.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Nosys)

### Nosys

Function not implemented; this indicates that the system is missing some functionality.

[§](https://gtk-rs.org#variant.Failed)

### Failed

Does not correspond to a UNIX error code; this is the standard “failed for unspecified reason” error code present in all #GError error code enumerations. Returned if no specific code applies.

# register_shared_type in glib::subclass::shared - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/latest/docs/glib/subclass/shared/fn.register_shared_type.html

`pub fn register_shared_type<T: `[SharedType](https://gtk-rs.org/trait.SharedType.html)>() -> [Type](https://gtk-rs.org/types/struct.Type.html)## Expand description

Register a boxed `glib::Type` ID for `T`.

This must be called only once and will panic on a second call.

See [ Shared!](https://gtk-rs.org/derive.Shared.html) for defining a function that ensures that
this is only called once and returns the type id.

---
